items.title: 25.3.2 The Loss of Energy between Trophic Levels

source_refs.note: Topic 25.3.2 with the Tidbit (PDF 234-235); Figure 25.5 is replaced by an original diagram, and the energy example is given as a table.

blocks.text: There are generally three or four trophic levels in an ecosystem. Producers convert only about 1-2% of the solar energy falling on them into the chemical energy of organic matter, and only about 10% of the energy at each level passes to the next; the rest is lost at each level, so very little usable energy remains after it has passed through the organisms of the different levels.

blocks.alt: A consumer drawn as an oval: an arrow brings in food eaten; arrows lead out to faeces (not absorbed), respiration (lost as heat) and growth (new body tissue, available to the next level).
blocks.caption: Where a consumer's food energy goes (original diagram after Figure 25.5).
blocks.long_description: Not all the energy a consumer eats reaches the next trophic level. Part is never absorbed and leaves in faeces, much is used in respiration and lost as heat, and only the part built into new body tissue (growth) can be passed on when the consumer is eaten. This is why only about 10% of energy passes from one level to the next, and why short food chains are more energy-efficient than long ones.

blocks.title: Tidbit: short chains are efficient
blocks.text: Short food chains, with fewer trophic levels, are more energy-efficient than long ones, because energy is lost as heat at every transfer.

blocks.prompt: If producers fix 50,000 kcal, about how much reaches secondary consumers?
blocks.explanation: About 10% of 10%: 50,000 to 5,000 (primary) to about 500 kcal (secondary).

items: Producers store 1-2% of sunlight; about 10% passes to each next level.
10,000 to 1,000 to 100 to 10 kcal; short chains waste less energy.
